messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Heavy Makeup: heavy make-up
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Vignette:
Leilani is a fifty-six-year-old married woman from a Pacific Islander community who works as a case manager at a faith-based social ministry in her small city. Two years ago, during a church event she had helped organize, a respected deacon—a man she had known for a decade—cornered her in a supply room after the evening service. She had been feeling light, relieved that the event had gone well, laughing with a friend moments before. He locked the door, and she remembers thinking, *This can’t be happening, this is a safe place*. The assault happened quickly, and afterward he said, “You’ll get over it, it’s not a big deal.” She never reported it.

In the months that followed, Leilani’s life contracted. At work, she now insists her desk be placed near the main exit and refuses to sit in the back office that has no second door. She tells herself it’s just a preference, but she knows she is scanning every room she enters for an escape route. When she feels happy or relaxed—the warmth of a sunny afternoon, a moment of laughter with her husband—a sick dread rises in her throat. She has come to believe that letting her guard down is what made her vulnerable; happiness is the doorway through which danger entered. So she stays tense, on purpose, because tension feels safer. At home, she checks every lock three times before bed, sometimes getting up in the middle of the night to verify the back door again. Her body is constantly wound: her shoulders never drop, her jaw aches from clenching. She describes it as “waiting for the next thing.”

To manage the distress, she has developed habits that worry her. After a hard day, she eats large amounts of comfort food—sometimes a whole pizza, a pint of ice cream—until she feels numb and slowed down. The heavy meals help her fall asleep, but she has gained weight and her doctor has expressed concern about her blood pressure. She has also started wearing heavy makeup every day, foundation and concealer applied thickly, even on weekends. It is not about vanity; she feels exposed without it, as though her face gives too much away. She believes the makeup is a kind of armor that makes her less likely to be noticed or approached.

The memory of the assault plays like a film she cannot stop. It is extremely clear: the smell of floor wax, the feel of the door handle pressing into her back, the deacon’s cologne. The memory intrudes at unexpected moments—while she is washing dishes, or sitting at her desk trying to focus on a client’s file. She has no control over when it starts, and she sometimes loses time re-living it. She has come to think that a different woman—stronger, more decisive—would have stopped it from happening, would have said something, would have fought back. That thought has reshaped how she sees herself. She used to define herself by her ability to help others: she was the one parishioners called when they needed a ride to a shelter, someone who could talk a troubled teen down from a rage. Now she feels hollowed out, no longer capable of that work. She avoids meeting with clients alone, especially men who are about the deacon’s age or build. She has delegated most of her direct casework to a younger colleague, making excuses about paperwork. Deep down, she is convinced there is something fundamentally wrong with her, some defect that made her the one this happened to.

What finally brought Leilani to therapy was a panic attack in the grocery store last month. A man in the next aisle laughed loudly, and she had to drop her cart and walk out. Her husband, who knows something happened but not the details, begged her to talk to someone. She is afraid that if she starts talking, she will break apart entirely. But she is also tired—tired of eating to calm the memories, tired of checking locks, tired of the film that plays in her head every night. What she hopes, though she cannot say it aloud yet, is that someone might help her understand why she feels this way—and maybe, just maybe, help her feel safe enough to stop living on guard.
